title: Otis Rush, Grateful Dead, Canned Heat at the Fillmore
lede: Wes Wilson’s Fillmore poster of February 1967: a woman’s profile whose hair becomes rippling bands of lettering that fill the whole sheet.
summary: Wes Wilson, 1967. Band names swell inside flowing hair, in pink, gray, and black on white.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.527-2004 (IIIF, 1183 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Catalogue data read on the V&A and Library of Congress records. Cooper Hewitt (1979-34-28) returned HTTP 403 to scripts, so its record is known only through its 2018 blog post. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The type trait in its purest form: Wilson’s lettering bends and swells until the band names become the hair of the figure. The palette is the exception: pale pink and gray on white, not vibrating complements.

context: The V&A catalogues it as psychedelic poster #51 by Wes Wilson, colour offset lithograph, 56.7 × 34.6 cm, and describes it as a “pink, green and black image of a female face in profile” with the text “within her hair”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O108984/).

The Library of Congress holds a copy printed by West Coast Lithograph Co., gift of Bill Graham (POS - US .W5578, no. 8). [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2014647489/). Cooper Hewitt holds another (1979-34-28) and describes “pale pink and grey” rather than intense hues, a “dense, crowded composition”, and lettering that blurs into the undulating strands of the image. [Cooper Hewitt](https://www.cooperhewitt.org/2018/10/23/deliberately-disorienting/).

Wilson (1937–2020) designed Bill Graham’s Fillmore posters in 1966 and 1967 and is credited with the melting, moving lettering; he took the space-filling block letters of Alfred Roller as a model. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Wilson).
observed: A woman’s face in profile looks left from the lower middle of the sheet. Her face is drawn in dotted contour lines like a topographic map.
Her hair streams to the right as alternating bands of black, pink, gray, and white. Each band carries lettering: OTIS RUSH, GRATEFUL DEAD, THE CANNED HEAT BLUES BAND, the dates, and FILLMORE.
The letters are hand-drawn, with round counters and swollen strokes. They stretch to fill each band, so that letter height changes along a word.
The ground is white paper. Color is limited to pale pink, mid gray, and black.
Only the top line, BILL GRAHAM PRESENTS IN SAN FRANCISCO, and the ticket outlets at the bottom are in a plain sans-serif.
The imprint at lower left reads “Wes Wilson ©1967 Bill Graham” with number 51 and the printer, West Coast Lithograph Co.
interpretation: This is the rubric’s type rule taken to the limit: the lettering is the image. It also shows that the color rule is not universal. Many Wilson posters use two or three soft inks on white.
The two plain lines at top and bottom work as the legible frame around an illegible center, a useful model for screens.
borrow: Set display words inside flowing bands and let the band shape set the letter height.
Keep one plain line of practical text above and below a free display area.
Draw a face or object in contour lines so it matches the rhythm of the lettering.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. The poster carries a © 1967 Bill Graham notice.
